title_en: Why Schools Should Lock Away Phones
description_ru: Эссе-рассуждение в пользу запрета смартфонов на уроках: аргументы, возражения и компромиссное решение.
text:
When I was a teacher, I used to think that banning mobile phones in classrooms was a lost cause. Every ban I had seen seemed to end the same way: students hid their phones under desks, teachers wasted energy playing detective, and everyone went home annoyed. But after watching what has happened in schools that have introduced a strict rule, I have changed my mind. In my opinion, phones should be locked away for the whole school day, and the evidence for this is stronger than most people admit.

Let me start with attention. Researchers who study learning keep repeating the same simple point: the brain cannot do two demanding things at once. It only switches rapidly between them, and every switch costs time and energy. One experiment, which has often been quoted, found that students whose phones were merely lying on the desk, face down and silent, scored lower on a memory test than those whose phones had been left in another room. The phone did not have to buzz to be a distraction. Simply knowing it was there was enough to take the edge off their concentration.

Supporters of phones in class reply that teachers can make good use of them. Students can look up words, take photographs of the board and use educational apps. That is true, and I do not deny it. But the same device that contains a dictionary also contains games, videos, group chats and a hundred other temptations, all of which have been designed by very clever people to be as hard to resist as possible. Asking a fourteen-year-old to ignore them is like asking someone on a diet to guard a bakery. If a school needs a screen, it can provide a tablet that has been set up for learning and nothing else.

The second argument concerns the break times. Several head teachers have reported that, after a ban was introduced, the playground suddenly became noisy again. Children ran, argued, invented games and, rather inconveniently for the staff, fell over. One head teacher told a newspaper that the lunch hall, which used to be quiet because everybody was staring at a screen, had turned into a chaotic place full of conversation. She added that she had never been so happy to hear so much noise. Learning to talk face to face, to read a friend's expression and to cope with an awkward silence is not a luxury. It is a skill, and like any skill it needs practice.

The third argument is about fairness. Not every family can afford the latest model, and a classroom in which phones are everywhere can quickly become a place where status is measured in cameras and screen sizes. Bullying has also moved online, and it follows children into lessons. When messages and photographs can be sent in seconds, a humiliating moment in the corridor can be seen by hundreds of classmates before the next bell has rung. A phone-free school cannot end cruelty, but it can at least reduce the audience.

Of course, the critics have some fair points. Parents often say that they want to be able to contact their children in an emergency. This is understandable, and the solution is simple: the school office can pass on urgent messages, as it did for generations before mobile phones existed. Others claim that a ban simply teaches children to rebel, and that it would be better to teach them to use technology responsibly. I agree that digital literacy matters. But self-control is not taught by leaving temptation on the desk. We do not teach children to cross the road by throwing them into the traffic.

What does the evidence from real schools show? In several countries where a ban has been introduced, teachers say that lessons start more quickly and that fewer arguments take place. A study of schools in England reported that test results improved, particularly for the weakest students, who seemed to benefit most from fewer distractions. Not every study has found such dramatic effects, and I would be cautious about promising miracles. Still, even a modest improvement is hard to ignore, given that the policy costs almost nothing.

The way a ban is introduced also matters. Rules that are imposed without explanation tend to be resented. The best results seem to come when students, parents and teachers discuss the reasons together, and when the rule is applied consistently to everyone, including the adults. A teacher who checks messages in the middle of a lesson cannot expect much sympathy when he confiscates a pupil's phone. Simple storage, such as a locked pouch or a box at the classroom door, also works better than relying on willpower.

I do not believe that phones are evil, and I use mine all day long. My point is that school is one of the few places left where young people are asked to concentrate on something difficult for an hour at a time, and where they can be bored without being rescued. Those are valuable experiences, and they are being squeezed out of modern life. A school phone ban is not a war against technology. It is a modest attempt to protect time and attention, two things that, once lost, are very hard to get back.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Кончик языка слегка между зубами, воздух без голоса: не «с» и не «ф».
Задняя часть языка к мягкому нёбу, звук идёт через нос; не добавляйте «г» в конце.
Ударение ставьте на нужный слог: ударный слог длиннее, громче и выше по тону, остальные сокращаются.
Перед ударной гласной p, t, k произносите с лёгким придыханием, как маленький выдох.

questions.question: What did the memory experiment show?
questions.answer: Students whose phones were on the desk, even silent, did worse than those whose phones were in another room.

questions.question: What are the author's three main arguments?
questions.answer: Attention, face-to-face contact at break times, and fairness and less bullying.

questions.question: How does the author answer parents who want to reach their children?
questions.answer: The school office can pass on urgent messages.

questions.question: What makes a ban work better?
questions.answer: Explaining the reasons, applying it to everyone including adults, and using simple storage like locked pouches.
